The noun hurt means a feeling of pain — either inside your body, or more commonly, inside your heart. It is the word we use to name the experience of being wounded — physically or emotionally.

Think of it this way: when something damages you — whether it is a scraped knee or a cruel word from a friend — what you feel in response is hurt.

1. Emotional Pain (The Most Common Meaning)

This is by far the most frequent use of "hurt" as a noun. It refers to the deep, inner pain you feel when someone has wounded your feelings — when you have been let down, disrespected, betrayed, dismissed, or treated unkindly by someone whose opinion matters to you.

This kind of hurt is not just sadness. It carries a very specific flavour: it is the pain that comes from feeling wronged by another person. It almost always involves a relationship — a friend, a parent, a partner, a colleague. Hurt in this sense says: "What you did (or said) damaged me."

"She tried to smile, but the hurt in her eyes was impossible to hide."
"He carried the hurt of his father's rejection for many years."
"I could hear the hurt in her voice when she spoke about it."

Notice how in these examples, "hurt" is not just pain in general — it is personal, relational, and directed. Someone caused it.

2. Physical Injury or Pain (Less Common)

As a noun, "hurt" can also refer to a physical injury or the physical sensation of pain. However, this use is less common in modern everyday English. People are far more likely to say "injury," "pain," or "wound" when talking about the body. The noun "hurt" in a physical sense appears more often in older literature, or in informal speech.

"He walked with a slight limp, trying to shake off the hurt in his ankle."
"The child cried, clutching the hurt on her arm."

You will understand this use if you encounter it, but you are unlikely to need to produce it yourself very often.

3. Harm or Damage (Formal / Old-Fashioned)

In a more formal or slightly old-fashioned register, "hurt" as a noun can mean harm or damage — the idea that something caused a negative effect on a person, group, or situation.

"No hurt was intended by his words."
"It does no hurt to ask."
"The scandal caused lasting hurt to the organisation's reputation."

In this sense, it is close in meaning to the words "harm" or "damage." You will mostly see this in formal writing or in classic literature.

This is a subtle but important point.

When "hurt" refers to emotional pain as a general feeling, it is uncountable — you cannot put "a" in front of it or make it plural.

✅ "There was so much hurt between them."
❌ "There was so much hurts between them."

However, when "hurt" refers to specific, individual experiences of emotional pain — particular moments or events that wounded someone — it can be used as a countable noun and made plural.

✅ "She had to let go of all the old hurts from her childhood."
✅ "Years of small hurts had slowly destroyed their friendship."

In this plural form, "hurts" means individual instances of being emotionally wounded — specific memories or events that left a mark.
The Feeling of Hurt — Up Close

To really understand this word, it helps to understand what emotional "hurt" feels like as an experience, because the word is used to capture something very precise.

Hurt is the pain that sits between sadness and anger. When you feel hurt, you feel:

  • Wounded — as if something inside you has been cut or bruised
  • Disappointed — someone or something did not treat you the way you deserved or expected
  • Vulnerable — your trust, love, or openness was not respected

Hurt is different from anger (which is outward and reactive), different from grief (which is specifically about loss, especially death), and different from general sadness (which does not require another person to have caused it). Hurt is almost always the result of what someone else did or said to you.

This is why we often talk about hurt using the language of wounds and medicine:

  • "The hurt ran deep." (It was a serious wound.)
  • "Old hurts that never healed." (Emotional scars from the past.)
  • "She nursed her hurt in silence." (She quietly dwelt on her pain.)
  • "It took years to get past the hurt." (To recover from the emotional injury.)

Here are natural, everyday ways "hurt" appears as a noun, so you can recognise and use them confidently:

  • "the hurt in someone's eyes/voice" — visible or audible emotional pain
    "I could see the hurt in his eyes."*
  • "feel the hurt" — to experience emotional pain
    "She didn't show it, but she felt the hurt deeply."*
  • "hide the hurt" — to conceal your emotional pain from others
    "He was always good at hiding the hurt."*
  • "cause hurt" — to wound someone emotionally
    "She never meant to cause him any hurt."*
  • "old hurts" — emotional wounds from the past
    "They had to talk through a lot of old hurts before they could move on."*
  • "no hurt intended / no hurt meant" — no harm or offence was meant
    "Please don't take it the wrong way — no hurt was intended."*
  • "deep hurt" — strong, serious emotional pain
    "There was a deep hurt inside her that she had never talked about."*

WordWhat makes it different

Pain is broader and more physical. You can have pain in your knee, your head, your stomach. "Hurt" (as a noun) is more personal and more emotional in modern usage.

Grief is specifically the pain of loss — usually the death of someone you love, or the end of something deeply important. Hurt is more general and relational.

Anguish is more intense and overwhelming than hurt — it implies extreme suffering, often physical or desperate. Hurt is quieter and more personal.

Wound (as a noun) is mostly physical. But when used metaphorically — "the wounds of the past" — it overlaps very closely with "hurt."

Offence is specifically the feeling that someone has violated a rule of respect or decency. Hurt is the pain that often results from being offended. They are related, but hurt is the feeling; offence is more about the act.

If you ever forget everything else, remember this:

Hurt (noun) = the pain — especially emotional pain — that results from being wounded by what someone said or did.

It is the quiet ache in your chest when a friend betrays you, the sting in your heart when someone dismisses you, the lasting bruise left by years of unkindness. It is personal, it is real, and it almost always involves another person.
